name: Toulouse deformity (bandeau)

card.summary: The bandeau was a French peasant custom of tightly wrapping newborns' heads, producing the elongated 'Toulouse deformity' skull shape, a historical case of head shaping.
card.note: Historical practice; infant head binding is associated with asymmetry and other harms.

quick.overview:
Bandeau was a traditional practice in rural France in which a newborn's head was tightly wrapped and padded with bands of cloth. The resulting elongated skull shape became known as the Toulouse deformity.

It matters to appearance culture as a documented example of the head and skull shape being altered in infancy. It persisted sporadically into the early twentieth century and was not apparently aimed at beauty: scholars describe the shape as an unwanted result of a protective custom.
quick.how: Historically, the wrapping was applied shortly after birth by families as a way to protect the head from knocks and accidents. It is a historical practice, and no modern use is described here.
quick.risks: Cranial deformation in general can cause marked asymmetry, and bleeding, infection or tissue necrosis where compression is severe. After infancy the effects are partly lost as the body compensates through growth.

lead: The bandeau was a peasant custom in France, most associated with the Toulouse area, in which an infant's head was tightly wrapped and padded soon after birth. The skull shape it produced is called the Toulouse deformity.[1]

Unlike earlier European and global traditions of deliberate head shaping to signal status or beauty, the Toulouse form is described as an unwanted result of a practice meant to protect newborns from impacts. It persisted sporadically until the early twentieth century.[1]
The French term bandeau is also used in surgery for the supraorbital bar in craniosynostosis repair, which is a separate meaning.[2]

paras: A baby's head was tightly wrapped and padded shortly after birth, a rural custom intended to protect against impact.[1] Scholars have noted that earlier observers pitied such children, believing old European customs had lowered their intelligence.[1]

Artificial cranial deformation in general can lead to strong cranial and facial asymmetry, and to bleeding, infection and necrosis of compressed areas. After infancy the effects progressively lessen as adaptive growth compensates. One study of Peruvian samples found no significant difference in cranial capacity between deformed and normal skulls.[1] Janot and colleagues studied facial adaptation in the Toulouse deformity.[1]
No studies found on the Toulouse deformity as a modern intervention. Historical anthropological work, such as Delaire and Billet (1964) and Janot et al. (1993), describes the skull form.[1]

timeline.event: Delaire and Billet publish a study of the Toulouse deformity.[1]
Janot et al. study facial architecture in the deformity.[1]
